title: Week 1: Build a talking box
summary: Turn a cardboard shipping box into a robot whose mouth moves when it talks. A servo and a Raspberry Pi Pico do the moving; a Deepgram voice agent in Chrome does the listening, thinking and talking. Log in, plug in, no coding.
detail: Fold a box, cut a mouth flap, glue in a servo and a paperclip linkage, then plug the robot into your laptop. Everything else happens on this page: give it a personality, pick a voice, tune how long it waits before answering, and let it check the weather and read a calendar. The mouth opens and shuts in time with its voice. Finish by filming a clip of your robot talking.
outcome: A cardboard robot on your table that holds a real conversation, moves its mouth as it speaks, checks the weather and reads a calendar, plus a clip of it to share.
prereqs: A laptop with Google Chrome. Safari and Firefox can't talk to USB devices.
A free Deepgram account and API key. Use the sign-up QR code at your table.
A USB port on your laptop. We have USB-C adapters if you need one.
Everything else is on the table: box, servo, Pico, jumpers, paperclip, tape, glue gun and cable.
artifact: A talking cardboard robot with a moving mouth, running the attendee's own prompt and voice, and a short video of it.

slides.title: Talking Robot Box
bullets: A shipping box, one servo, one tiny computer.
By the end of lunch it talks, and its mouth moves when it does.
No coding. Log in, plug in, talk.
slides.note: Hold up a finished robot and have it say hello. That's the whole pitch.

slides.title: What each robot needs
bullets: ☐ 1 × 8×8×8 inch shipping box, still flat
☐ 1 × MG90S micro servo, with its horns and screw
☐ 1 × Raspberry Pi Pico H (pins already on), loaded with the robot program
☐ 3 × male-to-female jumper wires
☐ 1 × USB-C to micro-USB data cable (not charge-only)
☐ 1 × jumbo paperclip
☐ Packing tape and a marker
Bring: a laptop with Chrome, and your Deepgram key
slides.note: Shared per table: 1 hot-glue gun and glue sticks, 1 pair of scissors or a box cutter. Helper table: spare data cables, USB-C to USB-A adapters, 2–3 spare loaded Picos, spare servos, extra paperclips. Pack the Picos already loaded with the robot program, and test each one with Connect robot before class. A charge-only cable is the top reason a robot won't connect.

slides.title: Fold the box
bullets: Fold the box along the folds that are already there.
Tape the bottom flaps shut. That side becomes the back of the head.
Turn it so the open end faces you. That's the face.
Cut off the two small side flaps on the open end. Keep one of them.
slides.note: Done when: the box stands on its side with the open end facing you and only a top and bottom flap left.

slides.title: Make the face and mouth
bullets: Glue the top flap shut. That's the face.
Put a strip of tape across it and draw the eyes on the tape.
The bottom flap is the mouth. Its fold is the hinge, so leave it loose.
Glue a piece of the cut-off flap inside the mouth, sticking up, as a tab.
slides.note: Done when: the mouth flap swings open and shut on its fold, and the tab is stuck firmly to its inside.

slides.title: Add the servo
bullets: Push the white horn onto the servo.
Hot-glue the servo to the floor of the box, near the front, horn on top.
Bend the paperclip into an L.
Hook one end through a hole in the horn, and push the other end through the tab.
Turn the horn by hand: the mouth should open and shut.
slides.note: Done when: turning the horn gently by hand opens and closes the mouth. If it binds, bend the paperclip, don't force the servo.

slides.title: Wire it up
bullets: Orange or yellow servo wire to GP15 (pin 20, bottom left with the USB at the top)
Red wire to VBUS (pin 40, top right)
Brown wire to GND (pin 38, two below VBUS)
Plug the Pico into your laptop with the USB cable
Check every wire twice before you plug in
slides.note: Hold the Pico with the USB port at the top and the pins facing you. Pin 1 is top left. Red on the wrong pin can damage the servo, so helpers should check wiring before anyone plugs in.

slides.title: Now the app
bullets: 1 Paste your Deepgram key
2 Connect the robot and press Wiggle the mouth
3 Set where the mouth sits shut and open
4 Write its personality and pick a voice
5 Start talking
slides.note: Walk the room. Most fixes are: the wrong browser, a charge-only cable, or the shut and open angles swapped.

slides.title: Show it off
bullets: Ask it the weather somewhere far away.
Ask what's on your calendar.
Try to make it laugh.
Film a 20-second clip and share it with #RobotLunchLab.
slides.note: Set up one well-lit corner with a plain background for filming.

slides.title: Week 2: a brain of its own
bullets: Bring your robot back next week.
A Raspberry Pi and a speakerphone take over from your laptop.
Then your robot can talk without a laptop attached.
slides.note: Ask everyone to take their robot home in one piece, or leave it on the shelf at The Hub.

flow.title: Bring your robot to life
flow.note: Use Chrome. Plug the robot in first, then work down the cards on the right.

troubleshooting: Connect robot shows no Pico in the list: the cable is probably charge-only. Swap it for a data cable from the helper table.
Connect robot does nothing at all: you're not in Chrome. Open the page in Chrome on the laptop.
It says the board did not answer: the Pico isn't running the robot program. Unplug it, plug it back in and connect again. If that fails, a helper reflashes it.
Could not open the USB port: another tab or app (often Thonny) has it. Close it and connect again.
The mouth moves the wrong way: swap the shut and open numbers on the sliders.
The servo buzzes or the Pico resets: the servo is drawing too much. Check the red wire is on VBUS, and only run one servo from a laptop.
The robot talks to itself: keep "Speaker is inside the box" switched on.
It cuts you off: raise Patience. It's slow to answer: lower it.
No sound: turn up the laptop volume and check the output device in system settings.
Deepgram stopped the session: check the key was pasted whole, and that the account has credit.

series.title: Physical AI Lab: Cardboard Robot
series.summary: A four-week build, one session a week. Week 1 turns a shipping box into a robot whose mouth moves when it talks. Week 2 swaps the laptop for a Raspberry Pi brain. Week 3 adds a battery so it runs with no cables. Week 4 gives it a neck so the head turns. Log in, plug in, no coding.
